intro: Fribourg's most famous tree is forty years old and stands where a five-hundred-year-old one did. The tilleul de Morat is tied to the legend of a messenger who ran from the 1476 battlefield waving a linden branch and collapsed in the Bourg, where the branch supposedly rooted. A vehicle struck the old tree in 1983 and it was felled. A cutting kept by the university's botanical garden went into the ground beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges the following year, and it is still standing.
meta_description: Fribourg's tilleul de Morat is a 1984 cutting of the medieval linden tied to the 1476 battle. Free, on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville.
question_meta: Fribourg's famous linden is a cutting of the medieval tilleul de Morat, planted in 1984 beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges. The legend and the record.
question_answer: The tree Fribourg is known for is the tilleul de Morat on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville in the Bourg quarter, and it is about forty years old rather than five hundred. It is a direct cutting of the original linden, recorded in the Bourg from the fifteenth century, which was struck by a vehicle in 1983 and had to be felled. The University of Fribourg's botanical garden had preserved the cutting; it was planted in 1984 beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges and stands there today, on a public square, free.
question_context: The legend runs like this. After Charles the Bold was beaten at Morat in 1476, a messenger ran to Fribourg carrying a linden branch cut on the battlefield, arrived, announced the victory and collapsed, and the branch he was holding took root where he fell. It is a good story, and it is a story. What is documented is the tree the story attached itself to: a linden recorded in the Bourg quarter from the fifteenth century, standing there for five hundred years, hit by a vehicle in 1983 and felled afterwards. The University of Fribourg's botanical garden had taken a cutting. That cutting was planted in 1984 on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges, and it is the tree standing there now, genetically the same plant as the one that fell and roughly forty years into a life of its own. Fribourg keeps the story working. A museum exhibition has been devoted to the linden, and for the battle's 550th anniversary in 2026 a second cutting is being planted about a hundred metres away on the Rue des Alpes.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Fribourg?
faq.a: The tree we map is not old. The tilleul de Morat was planted in 1984, as a direct cutting of a linden recorded in the Bourg from the fifteenth century, which was felled after a vehicle struck it in 1983.

faq.q: Is the linden of Morat the original tree?
faq.a: Not the original trunk, but the same plant. A cutting preserved by the University of Fribourg's botanical garden was planted on the square in 1984 after the old tree was felled.

faq.q: What is the connection to the Battle of Morat?
faq.a: Legend says a messenger ran from the 1476 battlefield to Fribourg with a linden branch, collapsed in the Bourg, and the branch rooted where he fell. The run is a legend; the tree that carried the story is documented from the fifteenth century.
Yes. It stands on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville, a public square in the Bourg quarter, beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges.

trees.story:
In 1476 a messenger is said to have run from the battlefield at Morat to Fribourg waving a linden branch cut on the field, collapsed in the Bourg quarter, and the branch took root where he fell. That is the legend. The tree on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville today is a cutting of the tree the legend was told about, planted in 1984, and it is about forty years old.

The original tilleul de Morat is recorded from the fifteenth century and stood in the Bourg for five hundred years. In 1983 a vehicle hit it and it had to be taken down. The University of Fribourg's botanical garden had kept a cutting, and that cutting went into the ground the following year beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges, where it still stands.

So this is a young tree at a very old address, which is both the honest description and the interesting one. Fribourg has not let go of the story: there has been a television segment, a museum exhibition devoted to the linden, and for the battle's 550th anniversary in 2026 a second cutting is being planted about a hundred metres away on the Rue des Alpes.

The square is public and free. The run is a legend, the felling is documented, and the tree in front of you is genetically the same plant as the one that fell.
